speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: BOBCAT VEHICLE
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ORDER FOR PILOT MODELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that a light armoured tracked carrier, known as the Bobcat, has been under development for the Canadian army for some time.
The Bobcat vehicle is designed in three basic forms; as an armoured personnel carrier, a cargo carrier and a self-propelled mount for the 105 millimetre howitzer, all built on a common chassis. These three basic types are further adaptable to meet many needs of the army such as weapons carriers, communications vehicles, ambulances, and for other operational and supply purposes.
In the past, mobility was provided by foot, wheels and tracks. The various components of the army moved separately but fought together. Now, because of the requirement to fight in widely dispersed small battle teams, this is no longer acceptable or practical, and battle teams must move, fight and live together. Therefore the basic philosophy behind the development of a family of vehicles with similar characteristics is to provide all parts of the team with an equal capability of movement.
The main features of these vehicles permit battle groups to move cross-country at 25 miles per hour, cross water obstacles without delay, and be protected from such battle hazards as small arms fire and shell fragments. In addition, a measure of protection is provided from effects of nuclear weapons.
Development having been successfully completed, it has now been decided to go into production of this vehicle. An initial order for 20 pilot models has been given to the original development contractor, the Canadian Car Company. The cost of the pilot models, plus production tooling, is estimated to be $3J million. It is expected that the pilot models and production tooling will be completed in about two years. At that time open tenders will be called for the production of a further 480 vehicles.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a statement to make to the house regarding the 1959-60 wheat pool. This account is in a surplus position and the government, on the recommendation of the Canadian wheat board, is authorizing an interim payment of 10 cents per bushel on all grades of wheat delivered to the pool between August 1, 1959, and July 31, 1960. I might add that producers delivered 377,438,000 bushels to the pool. The interim payment of 10 cents per bushel will therefore result in the distribution of approximately $37,744,000 to producers.
Yesterday I announced that the 1959-60 oat pool had been closed and a final payment would be made of $3,852,323. The interim wheat payment and the final oat payment will result in the distribution of approximately $41,600,000 to producers in the very near future. The oat payment is being made now, and cheques will be issued immediately for the interim wheat payment. Of the total wheat payment $23,678,000 will go to producers in Saskatchewan, $9,213,000 to Alberta and British Columbia, and $4,894,000 to Manitoba and Ontario.
The 1959-60 barley pool will be closed sooner than expected because of recent sales. Consequently the Canadian wheat board will report to the government on the conclusion of the interim wheat payment in regard to a possible closing date for the 1959-60 barley account.
I might add that I would have had copies of this announcement available for the press gallery but there has been a little smoke and confusion in the Confederation building this morning.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF SUPPORT FOR SECRETARY GENERAL
speechtext: I should like to direct a question either to the Prime Minister or to the Secretary of State for External Affairs; I am not sure who would like to deal with it. It is whether the government would reject the vicious attack made, according to reports, on the Secretary General of the United Nations by Moscow this morning, and repudiate this effort to destroy his position and give an assurance of the strong support of this parliament for the work of this dedicated international servant.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF SUPPORT FOR SECRETARY GENERAL
speechtext:
About noon today there were disturbing press reports, attributed to the Tass agency and as yet unconfirmed officially, that the Soviet union had withdrawn its recognition of Mr. Hammarskjold as United Nations secretary general and called for his dismissal. In addition, the Soviet statement demanded an end to the United Nations operation in the Congo within a month and


the withdrawal of all foreign troops. It condemned Belgium and called for the disarming and removal of all Belgian troops stationed in the Congo and for the arrest and trial of Mr. Tshombe and Colonel Mobutu.
The measures demanded are linked to the death of Mr. Lumumba and his two companions. The secretary general has been described as "an accessory to and organizer of" that act of violence. This Soviet statement appears to be a culmination of the bitter but unfounded attack launched by the Soviet union against the secretary general late last summer and all during the autumn session of the general assembly.
Under the charter the Secretary General of the United Nations is appointed by the general assembly upon the recommendation of the security council. Mr. Hammarskjold's reappointment in 1957 for a further five-year term had the support of all five permanent members of the security council, whose recommendation was approved by the general assembly.
Any unilateral action by the Soviet government can have no legal effect on the position of Mr. Hammarskjold, but it is of course deplorable that at a time of grave crisis for the United Nations one of the permanent members of the security council should choose to withdraw its support and recognition from the chief administrative officer of the organization. This can only add greatly to the difficulties facing the United Nations in the Congo.
This is not the first time that the Soviet union has acted in this way. Mr. Hammarskj old's predecessor suffered much the same treatment, mainly because of the part which he necessarily played in relation to the United Nations action in Korea. Happily the United Nations survived that Soviet assault on its integrity, and the world's best hope lies in its survival of the present crisis.
For its part the Canadian government will continue its firm support for the United Nations effort in the Congo and for Mr. Hammarskjold, who in the face of the greatest difficulty has served the high principles and purposes of the charter with courage, determination and endless patience. His devotion to duty merits strong and full support from all member states who have the best interests of the United Nations at heart.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I thank the minister for the statement he has just made and ask if he does not agree that a major-though not, of course, the only-difficulty facing the United Nations intervention in the Congo has been the policy of the U.S.S.R. itself?

subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE

speakeroldname: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide that the C.N.R. Railway Company may construct a line of railway from a point at or near mile 72 of the Kiask Falls subdivision to Mat-tagami lake, in the province of Quebec, and to authorize temporary loans to the company out of the consolidated revenue fund, not exceeding $9,660,000 to enable the work of construction and completion of the railway line to proceed forthwith; and to authorize the company to issue and the governor in council to guarantee securities to finance the expenditures upon the said line up to the said figure.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Rea in the chair.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement?

subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my statement will be rather brief because I think the resolution is relatively self-explanatory. I will have more details to give on the bill when we reach second reading.
This resolution is to approve the introduction of a bill to authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to construct a railway line in the province of Quebec from a point located about 72 miles north of Bar-raute on the line of the Canadian National between Barraute and Chibougamau, in a northwesterly direction to a point in Galinee township, a distance of about 60 miles. The 90205-6-1281
Canadian National Railways main function of this line would be to carry base metals from properties owned by Mat-tagami Lake Mines Limited near Mattagami lake. The line would eventually also serve a townsite of 3,000 to 5,000 people and would aid in the development of a potentially large mineral and pulpwood area. Its cost of construction is estimated at $140,000 per mile, or a total of $8,400,000.
Mattagami Lake Mines Limited plans to begin its mine production at the end of 1962 and will need rail service by that time. Since the construction of the line would take about two years to complete the committee will appreciate the importance of giving consideration to the legislation as soon as possible.
The bill which will follow the resolution will empower the Canadian National Railways to spend a sum not exceeding $9,660,000 on the construction of the line. This sum represents the estimated cost of construction which I mentioned earlier, plus 15 per cent for contingencies. The bill will also contain financial provisions similar to those adopted in the past for railway branch lines, and provide for the making of temporary loans by the government to enable the work to proceed forthwith and for the government's guarantee of the railway's securities issued in respect of construction.
When, in the course of the last session, my predecessor spoke in support of a resolution for the construction of the Toronto project by the Canadian National, he indicated that the government viewed with favour and proposed to give continued encouragement to capital projects that are submitted by the railway management and that can be recognized as self liquidating. The present project is of that category. The economic appraisal that has been made demonstrates that the railway revenue to be received from traffic engendered by the line will not only meet all expenses of operation and maintenance, the cost of handling such traffic on the remainder of the system, and amortization and interest on the cost of construction of the line, but will also produce a substantial annual surplus. The proposal is therefore one which will help in developing the resources of this country, and is also a sound one from a purely economic standpoint. I trust it will commend itself to all hon. members.
Perhaps the committee will permit me to add that when the bill that will follow the resolution has been given second reading I propose to move that it be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution now under discussion divides itself into

Canadian National Railways three parts. The first concerns the construction by the Canadian National Railway Company of a line from mile 72 in the vicinity of Kiask falls to Mattagami lake. The next is the expenditure involved, namely $9,660,000. The third part of the resolution has to do with authorization to the Canadian National Railways to guarantee certain securities.
Since this is the first piece of legislation which the new Minister of Transport has brought before us I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating him upon his appointment. I do so because I think the hon. gentleman is fortunate in having what in my opinion is perhaps the best portfolio in the service of the government. The hon. gentleman is also fortunate, I believe, in the quality of the officers he has in that department. All of them, from the deputy minister, Mr. Baldwin, right down to those who have less important tasks are loyal officers, and if the minister follows their advice I am sure he will not often go wrong.
I should next like to thank the hon. member for Villeneuve, who will make the main contribution from the opposition but who has allowed me to speak before him because of an engagement I have outside the committee.
This railway line is one which immediately commends itself to the opposition and for obvious reasons, such as I shall outline in a moment.
The railway is being built in one of the most promising areas of Canada. From the standpoint of mineral and other natural resources it is one of the finest areas in the province of Quebec. I refer to the Abitibi country. That region is one of the richest in natural resources in our province. Almost anything can be found in that area. There are good agricultural lands, minerals of all sorts including gold, copper, lead and zinc; there are tremendous reserves of forests, and above all there is hydroelectric energy in great potential.
It is the variety of these natural resources of all kinds which make this region interesting from the point of view of transportation and railway development. However, in order to assist in the development of the area an adequate system of transportation is necessary, because this area is not only far removed from the markets to which their products go but also because the rivers flow in a northerly direction whereas the products must move to the south. The development of this area goes back to the mid 1930's. It proceeded rapidly in the beginning, but that progress was temporarily interrupted during the war years which were responsible for a scarcity of materials.


In the post-war years private groups in the area established themselves because they were extremely interested in the development of the region. They were interested in its economic development and in the wealth that the natural resources such as minerals and forests could bring to their area.
At this point I think it would be well to pause for a moment to pay tribute to those private groups as well as their leaders for the tremendous interest they took in the economic development of their region. There is one who particularly stands out among them, Mr. Jean-Baptiste Lebel. I should like to pay tribute to him for the interest he has shown in this area and for the devotion which he and those associated with him gave to the development of this country.
The former Liberal administration had for many years foreseen the tremendous development which was about to take place in this region. Immediately following the war they began to make plans for a transportation system which have since been implemented in large part. The railway now under discussion before the committee is a branch line thereof.
The year 1946 saw the completion of the first railway line from Barraute to Kiask falls. A few years later it was clear that this line would not suffice and that additional transportation facilities would have to be constructed. Following the discovery of new mineral deposits it was necessary to extend the line, and in 1954 the government decided to add to the first line another line as far east as Cache lake and from there to Chibougamau and later to the lake St. John area at St. Felicien.
Upon construction of a railway from Chibougamau to St. Felicien, even at that time, it was quite clear that that line of railway, even though it was 300 miles long and even though it did help to develop a large portion of the natural resources, was not sufficient to give the area the railway system it required to take full advantage of its great potential assets. It was equally clear, sir, at that time that the line of railway from Senneterre to Chibougamau would sooner or later have to be extended by a branch line running in the direction of Mattagami lake.
However, at that time it would have been premature to have undertaken the construction of this branch line because the geological studies which were under way were not complete; neither were they conclusive. Furthermore-and I have no hesitation in making this statement- the former premier of the province of Quebec, the late Mr. Duplessis, was positively opposed to the establishment of a paper mill in that area which would have permitted the export of

forest products which are to be found in large quantities in the area of lake Mattagami. Under those conditions the construction of a branch line to Mattagami would not have been a profitable enterprise and, therefore, at that time would have been premature. Today, however, the situation in the province of Quebec is entirely different. It has changed materially to the point that the construction of this line is now a necessity.
We on this side of the house are happy to approve the resolution; we are happy to support it because, as I said earlier, it is a complement, it is an adjunct to the transportation system that was established during the years that we sat on the other side of the house. We are happy to support it not only because it is a good thing for the region but because it is the natural consequence of the railway line started by the former Liberal administration.
But, sir-and I say this without fear of contradiction-what we do object to, and object to strenuously, is that by the construction of this line the government is blowing its top and stating that it is inaugurating a great national policy as if nothing had been done in the way of railway development prior to the year 1957. My reason for making that statement is a speech made on television by the Prime Minister on January 18. In that speech he spoke of the great and extensive national development policy which was being inaugurated by this government to make Canada vigorous, vital and strong. When he came to the province of Quebec-he took each of the provinces in Canada one after the other to indicate what was being done by the government-here is what he had to say:
Well, there 300 miles of railway have been built by private enterprise.
That statement is inaccurate. There have not been 300 miles of railway built by private enterprise since this government has been in office. The only railway in the province of Quebec built by private enterprise on the north shore is that known as the Quebec -Labrador railway. It is 360 miles in length, and it was opened to the public on July 31, 1954, three years before this government took office.

subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext: What about the Port Cartier railway?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext:
I will come to that. The question now being put to me is, what about the Quebec Cartier Railway? Well, the Quebec Cartier line linking Port Cartier to Gagnon was opened on December 30, 1960, and is 193 miles in length; it is not 300 miles, as the Prime Minister said on television to all the
Canadian National Railways people of Canada. That statement, sir, was inaccurate and should be corrected in the house.
Furthermore, the Prime Minister went on to tell us about the new Mattagami branch project which was being inaugurated by the C.N.R. as if this was something extraordinary. Well, it is a line that we will support because it is a good thing for the area, but I suggest to those who sit on the other side of the house that in the first place they should not make inaccurate statements, and in the second place they should not get so excited about those tremendous developmental projects which were inaugurated long before they came into office.
This is another example of the way in which those who sit on the other side of the house proceed. Listen to this speech made by the Minister of Agriculture on television on February 19, 1960, when he was minister of northern affairs and national resources. Here is what he said, and this coming from a minister of the crown is really fantastic:
Generally speaking, in the last 50 years, there has not been any new railroad building by government, with the exception of the railway to Churchill and the P.G.E. The provincial governments were busy building roads to meet the needs of the people who lived in their provinces. Therefore, the forward motion of our economic expansion had ceased, and the country was settling down to a consolidating in areas where people lived.
How a responsible minister of the crown could make a statement of that kind when he knew, or should have known, that the former government built at least 700 miles of railway during the few years they were in office.

Mr. Chairman, the positive role of Canadian National Railways is very well exemplified by the resolution preceding the introduction of this legislation. We will support it, and we look forward to receiving more details from the minister at a later stage of the debate with respect to the economic information that led him and the cabinet to approve the legislation.
In the grand recital of the eight great projects which the former minister of transport gave, he mentioned one that has turned out to be not very economical, the line into Manitouwadge. A goof seems to have been
Canadian National Railways made by that magnificent Liberal administration, and we wound up having not one branch line but two branch lines into the base metal resource at Manitouwadge, neither of which is doing very well. Certainly there is not enough traffic for both of them. I raise this point simply to indicate that sometimes these grand schemes are not so good in the long run as they appear to be in the beginning.
One of the points that immediately come to mind, of course, is that this is a large base metal area into which the line is going. The minister probably knows that there are peaks and valleys in the world production of base metals. In recent years Canada has moved rapidly ahead in this field, and the long term prospects look good, but in the short run there is every indication that we may have a saturation of the markets for the very metals that are going to be coming from this particular area, something which may mean that the line will be built, the area will be opened up, yet the mines themselves will languish.
We should like to hear more about the economic projection in this particular direction. Certainly if the line is going to move pulpwood we should like to know more of what the prospects are of pulpwood delivery, to what mills the pulpwood will be going, and whether the crown lands in the Mattagami lake area are held by any particular concern; how they are being cut off, what is the cost of pulpwood that is coming out of there, and whether it can compete with the pulpwood that is much closer to the mills. One of the factors that we have discovered in our part of the country, where we have extensive pulp and paper production, as is the case in Quebec, is that the farther away you get from the mill, all the railway facilities in the world will not enable you to compete in putting your wood down at the mill. Once a wood haul gets to be over 150 miles or 175 miles in length it becomes an extremely high cost one, even with the most efficient kind of rail handling. Again perhaps the hon. member for Villeneuve can enlighten us on what the prospects are in this particular regard.
The cost of the railway line seems to be quite low per mile for the terrain that one normally encounters in the Laurentian area. We should like from the minister some assurance that this is the maximum figure of approximately $140,000 per mile.
The last point upon which I should like to comment in connection with this resolution is this. Before the royal commission on transportation the former Quebec government made a presentation-as I remember it, Hon. Daniel Johnson actually made it-and the

Canadian National Railways brief it seemed to me certainly expressed a chip on the shoulder attitude, an attitude indicating that the Canadian National Railways, the railways in general and the federal government had failed to come through for the province of Quebec in opening up its resource areas.
This matter has already been dealt with by the hon. member for Laurier in his own unique and Liberal way. I should appreciate hearing more about the position of the province of Quebec in this regard as it was expressed to the royal commission. It seems to me that we have two opposite positions, clarification of which I certainly should appreciate having. On the one hand we have a claim by the former minister that really the extension of rail lines in this country owed a tremendous amount to the great Liberal party, and in no place perhaps more than in the province of Quebec. This is his position. Now we have the brief before the royal commission, with which I am sure the minister is familiar, which indicates a completely different story.
As the hon. member for Laurier has pointed out, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture in his former role have taken a good deal of credit for a change in policy which is giving Quebec what it needs and wants. I think this would be a good time and a good occasion on which to have one of the government spokesmen from the province of Quebec set the record straight from their point of view; that is to say, set the record straight for those of us who do not wish to go down any particular party line and who would like to consider whether Quebec has been forced to languish without rail facilities in these resource areas, and if so why, and why the situation has changed at this time.
We think the resolution is a good one. We think the C.N.R. has a most positive role to play, and we only wish that this positive role could be emphasized more at a time when the road is under such severe criticism in other areas, and indeed when all railways are under such severe criticism. In northwestern Ontario the Canadian National Railways has played a marvellous part in the development of the resource industries, especially that of mining. Indeed, it seems to me that it is mining and the mining development that have made the C.N.R. through that part of the country much less of a money drain than many people feared it might be.
The Canadian National Railways has been under criticism by some of us in the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping for what we think is a retrogressive tendency in its dealings with labour and with the communities that fall within its particular orbit. There is not likely to be any question from the

communities that may be affected by this rail line about the need for it. I hope the minister is aware of the fact that disillusionment later comes to communities that get on rail lines. I refer to disillusionment as to the services they get, the number of employees that may be involved and the security of their employment. I hope the minister may be able to give us some indication later on in the debate with regard to the number of people who are going to be involved in work, the number of trains, the running crews, the maintenance crews and what this will mean in population and job terms for the area.
In summary, we should like to have more information than the minister has given us at this particular stage. If necessary we shall hope to bring this information out by questioning at a later stage when we are going through the bill section by section in committee.

Mr. Chairman, building that railway line will facilitate the development of natural resources in the lake Mattagami area.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) had only a few remarks to make on the matter. However, I noted that he proposed to supply further information when the legislation comes up for second reading.
It would be most interesting, for instance, to know the result of operations for the Barraute-Chibougamau line, and that other line which connects Chibougamau with St. Felicien.
Mr. Chairman, I would like the minister to tell us, on second reading, the earnings of the Canadian National Railways over those two sections, namely the line from Barraute to Chibougamau, and from that point to St. Felicien. In short, I would like to know the earnings for each of those sections.
Mr. Chairman, for the last five years there has been heavy prospecting in the Mattagami lake area. In fact, some 50 mining companies have been spending over 10 million dollars on prospecting and development work of all kinds, chiefly in the lake Mattagami district.
About a hundred mining properties have been tested. Geophysical, magnetic and electromagnetic work has been done. Geological surveys also were conducted on those sites, and diamond drilling took place on about 50 of the properties.
Therefore, for the past five years, a total of $10 million was spent in proving that some of those properties were well worth developing.
Two companies, among others, made major discoveries. The first and major one, the Mattagami Lake Mines Limited struck a deposit of about 21 million tons of metallic ore containing the following percentages: zinc: 12.76 per cent; copper: 0.68 per cent; silver, approximately 1.3 ounces per ton. While the gold content is low, it is not altogether valueless, assaying 0.018 ounces per ton.
On property bordering on that company's territory and belonging to the Orchan Mines

Limited a deposit of 6 million tons of ore has been discovered, of the following content: zinc, about 13 per cent; copper, 1.3 per cent; silver, 1.3 ounce per ton and gold 0.02 ounce per ton.
The enormous value of those two deposits is therefore readily realized.
The Mattagami Lake Mines Limited intends to build a plant with a capacity of 2,000 tons per day; the Orchan Mines Limited, on the other hand, proposes to build one with a daily capacity of 1,000 tons. Once those two plants are in production, they will put out the following quantities of metal per day: 375 tons of zinc, which means 750,000 pounds; 60,000 pounds of copper; 6,000 ounces of silver and 60 ounces of gold. Altogether, this represents a yearly production of 137,000 tons of zinc, 11,000 tons of copper, 190,000 ounces of silver and 21,900 ounces of gold.
At current prices for those metals the total yearly production is valued at about S40 million.
The zinc production of 137,000 tons represents 35 per cent of the total Canadian production at this time, which means therefore, that the Mattagami lake deposits are of outstanding significance.
I hope the house will welcome this resolution so that we way have the text of the bill as soon as possible.
Moreover, let us hope that there will be no delay in enacting the legislation, so that the contractor who has to carry out the work may start clearing operations as soon as possible.
The mining companies propose to develop the two most important deposits in the Mattagami lake area, the Mattagami Lake Mines Limited in the fall of 1962 and the Orchan Mines Limited in the latter part of 1963.
If the railroad is not completed by that date, mining development will naturally be delayed. Therefore, I hope that everything will be done so that this legislation may be passed with all possible dispatch.
Mr. Chairman, I have personally taken part in the development of that area. I am still keenly interested in this matter, even if the area involved is outside the constituency of Villeneuve. It is in fact located in the neighbouring riding, that of Chapleau (Mr. Martel), a vast territory.
We have been hearing about Mattagami for several years. It was mentioned in this house in 1954 at the time the building of the Chibougamau railway was being considered,
Canadian National Railways and the matter was raised on many other occasions when it was always pointed out that the natural resources of this area were practically unlimited. They are indeed almost unlimited because, besides the two deposits I mentioned earlier, in 1958, that is a year after the discovery of a deposit by the Mattagami Lake Mines Limited, another Canadian company, the New Hosco Mines, discovered another rather substantial copper deposit quite close to the Allard river, a few miles to the northwest of the Mattagami mines. This deposit will no doubt be also developed in the comparatively near future.
A little closer to Mattagami Lake Mines, to the northwest, another Canadian company, the Radio Uranium Mines Limited, made a fairly important discovery with diamond borings. I am convinced that at this place a workable copper and zinc deposit will also be discovered.
A bit farther to the northeast, the Con-nest company has traced another deposit which is not to be ignored since it contains a fairly high percentage of copper and zinc, even though of lower grade than others discovered so far.
As far as mining is concerned, this area has hardly been touched to this day.
And now, in addition to those mining resources, the Mattagami area has almost unlimited timber resources. As a matter of fact I read in a recent report that timber resources in the Mattagami area amounted to more than 50 million cords of wood immediately available. Hence the importance of making haste in trying to develop natural resources in this area.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) mentioned in his opening remarks one of the pioneers of northwestern Quebec who deserved all our admiration, Mr. Jean-Baptiste Lebel. In fact, Mr. Lebel, in the course of his numerous activities in northwestern Quebec, has always advocated development in the Mattagami lake area.
For years he has been dreaming of a pulp-wood industry there. Well, I believe that his dream is about to come true, since there has been talk of a very large lumber company from Quebec considering in the coming months the possibility of building a plant quite near to Mattagami lake, close to the eastern part of the area with which we are concerned. If this pulp-mill or paper plant is to built, it will probably require the construction of another branch line, from a point close to the Bell

Obviously the timber cut from those forests will be floated down those rivers as far as James bay, and much of it will be processed locally, where paper mills will be built. Needless to say that the manufactured product will have to be shipped either by boat for part of the year, or by rail in the winter months. Therefore, we expect the railroad to eventually reach James bay at Rupert bay.
A fact that must not be overlooked is that, in addition to the mining and large forest resources in the Mattagami area, that are found all along the major rivers flowing into James bay, there are also considerable iron ore deposits on the Great Whale river, a little farther north. Those deposits will one day be developed and the sensible procedure would be to transport the ore southward along the Nottaway river.
Thus, the construction of the Chibougamau railroad was simply the beachhead of the development of the natural resources in northwestern Quebec. By building this branch line to lake Mattagami, we are establishing a

second beachhead. That is why I repeat, as I said in my opening remarks, that I hope the house will support this resolution and that the members will assist in hastening all stages of the bill, so that construction may start as soon as possible.
Mr. Chairman, a few moments ago, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), referred to lumber concessions in the Matta-gami lake area.
In the immediate area around Mattagami lake, there have been no forest concessions, as yet. Those which have been officially established were located along Bell river, about half way between Senneterre and Mattagami. However, there is no doubt that if some companies decided to put up pulp mills there, the government would be able to guarantee them some lumber concessions to supply the pulp or paper mills for several years to come. There is no need to worry about that angle as the forest lots in the district, starting about fifty miles south of Mattagami lake and stretching towards the great north, have not been conceded yet. There are enough lumber resources in that area, I would say, to supply three or four paper or pulp mills.
Consequently, Mr. Chairman, I think that hon. members who are not familiar with northwestern Quebec districts will realize the importance of building that railway line. The cost will be under $10 million, whereas the two corporations I named at the start of my remarks, i.e., the Mattagami Mines Limited and the Orchan Mines Limited propose to spend over $40 million during the next three years.
We should also remember that the two corporations are ready to develop their own deposits; they also want that part-or rather the greater part-of those underground resources to be processed locally or, at any rate, within the province of Quebec.
For that reason, the two companies intend to build a zinc refinery with a daily capacity of 400 tons. Those two firms alone will produce 375 tons a day. It is therefore quite understandable that a zinc refinery with a minimum capacity of 400 tons a day is required because, in addition to the facilities of Mattagami lake, 200 additional tons of zinc are produced daily in various mines located nearby, in northwestern Quebec. It is therefore highly important that the zinc refinery
Canadian National Railways be established as soon as possible, and we hope that it will be built in the Mattagami lake district. However, there may be certain factors which could cause the companies to decide otherwise. As far as I know, however, the firms concerned believe that, if economic conditions are favourable, the refinery will be established in that area, or rather, we have been assured that it will, at any event, be erected in the province of Quebec, which is a most important decision.
Mr. Chairman, you can see how important is the development of the Mattagami area which, as I said, is the nerve centre of northwestern Quebec. I am convinced that with the co-operation of everyone, we could develop this area, not only for the benefit of its own residents, but also for the benefit of the citizens of the province of Quebec and of Canada as a whole.

Canada Elections Act CANADA ELECTIONS ACT

the second reading of Bill No. C-15, to amend the Canada Elections Act (age of voters).
He said: Mr. Speaker, while the bill in its form contains a number of technical amendments, the end it seeks is relatively simple, namely to reduce the age of qualification of electors from the present 21 years to 18 years. During the last session of parliament a complete revision of the Canada Elections Act was undertaken. The standing committee on privileges and elections made a complete perusal and review of the act and in that committee this subject matter was dealt with to a considerable extent. However, the committee was not of the opinion that it should recommend such a reduction to parliament.
As a preliminary comment I might add that in the committee itself there was some discussion about the question of legal age, as I understand it, of a person. It was to the effect that one under the age of 21 was not able to enter into a valid contract of purchase and the like, and the thought expressed was that these things should go hand in hand. It was thought that if the voting age was lowered there should also be a consequent reduction in the legal age. However, it was subsequently pointed out by members of the committee who were of the legal profession that this latter matter of the legal age, so called, is one of provincial jurisdiction rather than of federal jurisdiction, and I think perhaps we may only look at it in that light and in a general way.
A variety of reasons are put forward, to which I subscribe, as to why the age of electors should be reduced to 18. Perhaps the first one that comes to mind is that we have improved educational facilities. Over the years the average grade reached in school has been steadily increasing. I understand that the average person now reaches grade 10 or thereabouts. I understand that grade may perhaps increase further or that it may have increased since the last census. Because of improved communications more immediate contact with political events in this country and those in other parts of the world we are in effect approaching what is described as a smaller world. All in all, it means that our younger generations have increased opportunities to have firsthand knowledge almost of public affairs and of political matters

Canada Elections Act
not only in this country but in other countries of the world as well. With improved communication systems such as television, for example, the events that take place in other parts of the world are known to us almost immediately as they occur. I say that this quick means of communication gives our younger people a much better insight into political and public affairs and a more immediate knowledge and better understanding of them than was possible 20 years or 30 years ago.
I made inquiries of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), who is in the teaching profession or who practised the teaching profession before he reached this place, although some people may doubt whether or not he engages in that sort of activity. Nevertheless, there is a situation that prevails in Ontario and I understand that it prevails in Manitoba, from information given to the committee last year by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mand-ziuk); and I am given to understand that it prevails in other provinces also. In Ontario, it is not uncommon to find people entering the teaching profession at the age of 17, 18 or 19 or thereabouts. These teachers in fact engage to some extent in the teaching of history and of current affairs but they themselves are not in a position to vote.
It is not uncommon to find university students of the age of 18 or 19 or thereabouts. In universities the question of political activities is gone into far more extensively. For instance, just the other day a group of political science students from Queen's University visited the parliament buildings. Many of them were under the age of 21. Mock parliaments are in existence in practically all the universities in the land and, I understand, to a slight extent even in the latter years of high school in some places. All of these things tend to put the individual who is under the age of 21- that is the legal age to vote-in closer and more immediate contact with public affairs and to give him a better understanding of those affairs than was possible a number of years ago.
We consider that a person of the age of 18 is mentally and physically capable of participating in the war effort when it has been necessary in the past to draw him into that field of activity, and we still think in those terms. Likewise, I think we should consider that he is capable of exercising the same degree or a similar degree of political judgment that a more mature person or a more elderly person might be capable of exercising.

1 realize that people who are in the armed forces can vote. However, I should perhaps emphasize that what I am getting at is this. If parliament is of the opinion that persons of the age of 18 have the abilities, mental and physical, necessary to participate in the armed forces, then we should also consider that they have the qualities and the abilities necessary to participate in electing candidates. I consider that extension of the right to vote is merely an extension of our right in a democracy by providing these persons of 18 years of age an opportunity to participate openly and fully in electing members of parliament to represent them in the House of Commons.
The speed-up in our economic activities coupled with intensified education tends to draw people into the working force at a younger age than formerly. It tends to draw them into marriage at a younger age. It tends to draw them into the taxation field at a younger age by their mere entry into the working force. I submit that it tends to draw them into political activity as well, especially in some provinces in Canada which have a lower voting age than that which is provided under our Canada Elections Act.
I might perhaps in that regard make brief reference to some information which was given to the committee on privileges and elections during the last session and which was also entered on the record in a specific debate in this house during the last session. In the province of British Columbia and the province of Alberta the voting age is 19. In the province of Saskatchewan it is 18. In the province of British Columbia I participated in a provincial election as a candidate when the voting age was 19 and since that time I have participated in a provincial election in which I was not a candidate but which was held just recently, and the voting age was still 19.
We have found-and I am sure the same things have been experienced both in Alberta and in Saskatchewan-that there is a feeling of greater satisfaction on the part of the people in this age group in having the opportunity to participate in the great democratic process of electing M.L.A.s and governments in those provinces. There do not appear to be any difficulties whatsoever that have flowed from the electors in those provinces having the right- to vote at the ages I mentioned.
Perhaps I could also indicate briefly the situation in other countries and other states from the material which was placed on

Canada Elections Act
Hansard last session. I would point out that the voting age is 18 in the states of Georgia and Kentucky in the United States of America; in Bulgaria; in Venezuela; in Mexico, if married; Bolivia; in Costa Rica if one is married or a teacher; and also I understand in the Union of South Africa, although I would not use that political situation there as an argument to warrant our following suit.
In the state of Alaska it is 19; in Costa Rica, for other than married men and teachers, it is 20. There are a great many countries like Great Britain and New Zealand where the age is 21. There are some countries in which the age is higher than 21, notably Turkey, where it is 22; Denmark, where it is 23; and the Netherlands, where it is 25. This is information compiled from the Statesman's Year Book of 1959. I do not know what the current situation is, but I assume it is somewhat the same.
At the last session, Mr. Speaker, you will recall, as will other hon. members, that when we were considering third reading of the bill to amend the Canada Elections Act the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) moved a technical, procedural type of motion that the bill should not be read a third time then but should be referred back to committee for the purpose of reconsidering this question of lowering the voting age.
We had a division in the house on that amendment. The Liberals and ourselves voted together to, in effect, reduce the voting age. The Conservative members voted that it should not be reduced at that time, and there was some reasoning given as to why that course of action was followed by the Conservative members who participated in that division.
That reasoning was given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and perhaps I might be allowed to quote some of his remarks from Hansard of last year in this regard. I use them to say that I accept the invitation extended by the Prime Minister last session and think it is perhaps the course that we might well follow at this stage in order to bring a full, complete discussion and consideration of this matter in accordance with the time honoured practice of dealing with amendments to the Canada Elections Act.
I will quote from the remarks of the right hon. Prime Minister as reported at page 6279 of Hansard of July 14, 1960. Here the Prime Minister, referring to the amendment to which I referred earlier, said:
I think it is one of those things that might very well be studied in detail by a committee at a subsequent session of parliament,-
Then he said:
In a subsequent session I will join with hon. members in giving the membership of the house an adequate opportunity to fully explore all the considerations relative to this question;-
I think the course suggested by the right hon. gentleman on July 14, 1960 should apply to this session. This is a subsequent session and I think this would be a proper course to be followed. I have indicated on other occasions this should be the course to be followed with all public bills introduced by private members, but especially is it so in this case because we have the endorsation of that course by the right hon. Prime Minister.
While he may quibble, as perhaps he sometimes does, as to precisely what he meant -he may quibble that this is not the subsequent session to which he referred-none the less this is a subsequent session and it is the first one since 1960. Because this is such an important matter, because it relates to the right of people in the nation to participate in electing members of parliament and governments, because of the reasons I expressed earlier, because this is so much an integral part of our maintenance of democracy I think this should be classified as the subsequent session to which the Prime Minister referred. While he and I may have differences of opinion about some things sometimes, on this one we are in complete accord. I think that after the bill has been given second reading-I do not think there is any doubt about its passage-it should properly be referred to the privileges and elections committee for adequate and detailed study.

Mr. Speaker, following the line of argument the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) was developing there is one matter that occurred to me following my perusal of the committee report of last year. I was a member of that committee. Unfortunately I was unable to be present the day this particular matter was discussed in the committee. However one thought occurred to me while the hon. member for Skeena was referring to the remarks of the Prime Minister. The hon. member made reference to what particular subsequent session might be the most appropriate time to examine this question. With the census being taken this year and with information which, to say the least, would be most pertinent to any examination of this question, perhaps the hon. member might restrain his enthusiasm for this inquiry until we have more comprehensive and more up-to-date information.

I recall that earlier in his remarks, when he was attempting to evaluate one aspect of this question, he made reference to the census and the fact that the results of that census would give us more complete and comprehensive information. I was interested both in reading the committee report last year and in the hon. member's discussion on the bill today.
One thing has always puzzled me, and perhaps the answer is available from some other hon. member who may be able to be of assistance in this regard. It has always been a source of mystery to me why the age of 21 came to be the age of legal responsibility. I can appreciate the relationship of the age of voting and the age of legal responsibility, but there seems to be a certain sanctity surrounding this particular age and I would be most interested if any hon. member could give me some assistance along this line.
The hon. member for Skeena referred to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). I was interested to find during a recent trip to Queen's University that a former student of the hon. member for Port Arthur was apparently unaffected by the socialistic leanings which one might expect to find in that hon. member's teachings. This student turns out to be a most active, lively, enthusiastic Conservative on the campus of Queen's. As a matter of fact, he happens to be the president or leader of the Conservative group on that campus.

speechtext: It just shows the teacher was broadminded.

I have had occasion recently to examine at first hand some of the political activities in the various universities of Canada. Late last fall I had the great privilege of visiting St. Francis Xavier University, Dal-housie, the University of New Brunswick in Fredericton, and Mount Allison University in Sackville. Certainly, if one can judge from the calibre, intelligence and capacity, particularly of the Progressive Conservative student groups on these campuses, there is no question or doubt in my mind whatsoever that the reduced voting age should be applied to each and every one of these students.
I can think of several good examples where from every other point of view they are qualified with room to spare, even though some of them have not yet reached their eighteenth birthday. It is interesting to consider what one might find as a result of lowering the voting age to 18 years of age and the accompanying impact on student life, particularly if an election took place during the academic year.

I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I had nothing whatsoever to do with this, but shortly after my visit to Mount Allison University a movement was started which resulted in banning all political activity on that campus. As I say, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it had nothing to do with my visit; the incident which precipitated this action took place before I arrived.
However, it is of more than passing interest to find that on the occasion of a new Liberal government taking office in New Brunswick one of the first things to happen is that political speech is to some extent stifled within the boundaries of that province. However, that is perhaps stretching the point a little. Getting back to the point of the university itself, it has been argued, and it was argued during my time as a student at Carle-ton College, that extracurricula affairs and in particular extracurricula political affairs had a damaging effect on academic standards. Perhaps there is some merit in that. It would be interesting to hear from some of the faculty members and university administrators concerning this aspect of the question.
In developing his argument the hon. member for Skeena also suggested that education, and the fact that we have, obviously, better informed young people in our universities today, perhaps has another side to it. The most impressive argument in this whole question has to do with the relationship of responsibility and privileges, and the age-old cry from people all over the world concerning taxation and representation. It seems to me that there is an almost unanswerable case put forward by a young man who is married and who is earning a living and raising children. It seems to me that a person in that specific situation, having those qualifications, cannot be deprived of a vote without a measure of injustice being done. This is along the same lines as the case which the hon. member mentioned where we allow a young person to join the armed services where he would theoretically be exposed to the bullets of the enemy, and yet deprive him of his vote at the same time. I myself happen to have joined the air force at the age of 17J and, frankly, some of my most vivid recollections are that on different occasions and in different situations I was deprived of certain rights and privileges which were extended to fellow citizens of 21 years of age.
Actually in practice most of the restraints of this kind were not rigidly enforced during the war years in this country to any extent, but the point is, as I say, that there is a strong case for the young man who is married and having children. But it seems to me, though perhaps the census figures might

contradict this statement, that young persons particularly embarking on a university education do not take on the accompanying responsibilities until later in life, and the more specialized the various fields of education become, particularly as far as medicine and other faculties are concerned, the older, it seems to me, are our graduates from those institutions before they begin to earn money, pay taxes, get married and have children.
However, there are countertrends, I know, and particularly in recent years in the United States there is a growing number of young people who anticipate this problem. A great many of them marry while at university and a rather impressive number in high school as well.
So much for the points raised by the hon. member for Skeena. As far as knowledge and appreciation of the political facts of life are concerned, political activity at the various universities is at an astonishingly high level. As I mentioned, I have visited a number of universities in the maritimes, Queen's University, and more recently still the University of British Columbia, the branch of the University of Alberta in Calgary, the university itself in Edmonton, and the University of Saskatchewan at Saskatoon where a large number of young students turned out to hear a speech which I happened to be making.
I suspect, and said so at the time, that seeing a real live Tory from Toronto way out in Saskatchewan many were perhaps interested to see if I had any horns growing out of my head. I reassured them on that point, but the point I am making is that at the university there, and later on in Winnipeg, I found a very high level of knowledge, background and interest, and in any of the discussions which took place, either in political science classrooms or in meetings over the traditional cup of coffee, I found that the calibre and the degree of information would stand up against many hon. members in this house. As a matter of fact on a couple of occasions I was chased up a tree, so to speak, and I have had to do a little homework since returning to the house to provide the answers to the questions that were raised.
It is interesting, too, how this political interest can develop. In connection with Queen's University I had been looking forward for some time to the opportunity to visit the Joyceville institution and also the women's prison in that city. I mentioned those institutions to this young group of Conservative students and found that a substantial number both among the young men and the young women present in the group was most interested, concerned and stimulated by the activity in this field in recent years, and as a result of our visits to those institutions many
Canada Elections Act
of these young people have indicated a desire to follow this subject up further with discussion groups and guest speakers. The most encouraging thing of all, it seems to me, was the interest expressed in the John Howard Society and the Elizabeth Fry Society.
On balance, as I say, I would certainly support this measure as it applies to the university students I have encountered in my own days at college and in more recent times. I notice that the hon. member who introduced the bill, the hon. member for Skeena, mentioned in the committee last year that he was not wedded to the idea of 18, that perhaps 19 would be an appropriate age. This is perhaps a matter purely of choice.
I examined this question and prepared a series of qualifications which perhaps it would be more desirable to follow if the voting age were to be lowered to 18; qualifications along the lines I have mentioned, such as being married or a breadwinner in a larger family or, at any rate, paying taxes in some form or other, but upon discussing this with several members and persons who have considerable experience in administrative aspects of government I find this would create more problems than it would solve.
Certain groups in our society which did not happen to be included would feel as some people felt concerning the advance poll before the committee on privileges and elections recommended amendments to the act concerning the question of voting at the advance poll. Hon. members will recall that this privilege was confined to fishermen, railway workers, and a few other select categories. When you make exceptions and establish certain categories you immediately create a situation wherein other groups feel they have an equal right and entitlement to this privilege and are being discriminated against if it is not granted to them. I think that trying to couple a reduction in the voting age with restrictions in qualifications would be, on balance, a fruitless pursuit.
Although I am in favour of the principle involved in this bill I feel it would be more prudent to follow the suggestion made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) during the last session and delay consideration of this question until we have the comprehensive, complete and up to date information which will be available when the census reports are published.

For my part. I should like very much to be able to vote at 18. The young men of my age are able to take a useful interest in the social and economic policies of their country or province- Furthermore, in granting young people the right to vote at 18 years of age. they will be given an opportunity to feel they are of some concern to the government. When you trust someone, you automatically increase his self-confidence and his will to assert himself.
And the other two students who expressed their views in that same article of La Presse, said approximately the same thing as the other two I have just quoted.
I was reading in the newspaper Le Devoir for February 9, 1960:
Any group which does not have a solid core of youth is doomed.
I say that if you try to keep young people out of politics, you run the risk of having them sooner or later stay away from politics for good.

The previous speaker has spoken at length about over 18 year old citizens and dealt mostly with university students. He probably forgot to mention that we have in this country an important group of 18 year old citizens who are on their own, who earn their living and pay taxes.
I am in agreement with the member for Skeena when he says that television, radio and other media for the dissemination of ideas have made such progress in the last 25 years that it can be said that our young people are generally more advanced today than before.
Thus, we have reason to believe that the citizen who for all practical purposes has left his home, is emancipated, legally speaking. If he goes to university, he is then attending an institution of higher learning and does not live at home any more. If, on the other hand, as I was saying, he has begun earning his living from this very moment and in a certain way he is considered as being of full age before the law and certainly in the eyes of his parents. Indeed, should a person marry before reaching 21, the mere fact of his marriage makes him fully entitled to emancipation, according to section 314 of the civil code, that is to say that the law considers him to be of full age. Moreover, section 314 of the civil code grants minors who are working the right to institute proceedings on their own behalf for recovering damages. In addition, a minor who is in business is considered to be of age in respect of any business deeds.
It is apparent that there is a tendency to emancipate those under age because it has been found by the legislator that today a youth of 18, unless he be a student, is already looking after himself. Therefore, if by what he is earning, he is having his share of the country's gross national revenue, he then becomes a buyer of goods and consequently a taxpayer. From the very fact that he is paying taxes directly or indirectly it may be argued that the minor is actually interested in public administration.
As the previous speaker said, there is a common saying, often quoted by the English and which moreover was one of the arguments for the great charter of the 13th century: No taxation without representation.
Let us not forget too that a minor who owns a car or holds a driving licence is liable to get entangled in legal situations no less seriously than those who have the right to vote.
I think it might be fitting also to add an argument that may sound rather sympathetic but is true nevertheless. Whenever the country is attacked, youths of 18 are the first called to defend it.

However, if the age of voters were brought down from 21 to 18, it would be necessary for the provincial government, at least for the government of Quebec, to amend section 324 of the civil code and set the majority age at 18 instead of 21.
Mr. Speaker, as I said, I support wholeheartedly the bill introduced by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), and I hope that in the not too distant future our 18 year old citizens will have the opportunity to take a greater interest in politics than they do at present and that they will be in a position, not only to serve political parties in their electoral campaigns but also to make their contribution to the administration of our country.

Mr. Speaker,
1 suppose when this question is put to each one of us we already have an opinion and then must search around in our hearts and minds to determine what basis there is for the attitude we have. This is essentially a basic question.
As I listened to the contributions made by the previous speakers this afternoon I found my mind wavering back and forth. I first took the position that there should not be a lowering of the age limit from 21 to 18 but after listening to some of the arguments advanced I changed my mind slightly but again reverted to my original position. As I talk, perhaps I will change my mind again.
Based on the earnest remarks of the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) it seems to me that one could make out an equally good case for the fact that the intellectual types he mentioned should not be accorded this specific privilege. I think there are two factors which must help us to determine voting ages or voting limits. One of these is the intellectual factor, the ability to study and comprehend public issues, and the other is the levelling of experience which puts some practicality in young men or young women. I do not think that factor should be taken lightly, Mr. Speaker.
There are gifted souls, very young ones and very old ones, who are able to grope intellectually and master problems, and yet there are also a large number of people-I wish I could phrase this much better than I am doing because I am doing it rather bluntly-who decide public issues from the rather practical standpoint, namely can the country afford to take this step, or would this be too costly to the taxpayers? Somewhere in between one reconciles these two points of view and, of course, that happens all the time.
We sit here in parliament. We have the eager visionary ready to dash in and cure any
Canada Elections Act
ill in the world with legislation and the massive spending of public money. Then, we have those who say, whoa, the remedy is not good enough. You will kill the taxpayer while you are doing it. I would think that this school of thought must have been in the minds of the legislators of Costa Rica and of Mexico when they reduced the voting age in their countries to 18 but applied certain strictures. For example, the people of Mexico who vote at the age of 18 must be married, and those from Costa Rica who vote at the age of 18 must be married men or teachers.
Without having the benefit of reading the debates of Mexico or of Costa Rica it seems to me that the legislators there had some serious thoughts on whether a person who had reached 18 was a fit and proper person to entrust with the most sacred privilege in a democracy, namely the right to vote. I think they came to the conclusion that somebody who had to go out and work for a living, scrape together the wherewithal to support a family was such a fit and proper person because he did have a certain amount of practical experience, knew something about handling budgets and all that sort of thing. I think that is an important thought to keep in mind and that is why I said, perhaps too bluntly, and perhaps I will get myself in trouble in the next university I go to and get run up a tree, as did the hon. member for York-Scarborough, that such a person who had intellectual gifts at 18 to weigh public issues may not have the practical experience to go along with them to justify the granting of the right to vote to him.
In the May 19 proceedings of the committee on privileges and elections, at page 323, is set forth the nine countries, states or provinces where they have the right to vote at the age of 18. I quote briefly from the record. The list includes two United States states, namely Georgia and Kentucky, one Canadian province, Saskatchewan; behind the iron curtain there is Bulgaria, although they might as well give them the vote from the cradle to the grave because it does not seem to make any difference in the turnout or the ratio at the polls. It is always 99 24/100 per cent for one party. I do not know how the other votes go. Most of the other countries are in North or South America, Venezuela, Mexico, Bolivia, Costa Rica and then the Union of South Africa. Therefore, by not adopting the measure this afternoon we will not exactly be turning our backs on a large and progressive step taken in a large number of countries. As I have indicated, only nine states have

Canada Elections Act
taken this step and two of them have applied certain strictures to the voting age of 18, namely Mexico and Costa Rica.
The hon. member who sponsored the bill also mentioned the matter of minority and majority, passing from the state of infancy to manhood or womanhood and said that it was purely a provincial matter. He fortified this view by some remarks made, I understand, by legal members of the committee on privileges and elections. I suppose this is a somewhat valid point except that it could cause confusion to split a person in two and say that legally he becomes of age when he is 21 but democratically he will become of age when he is 18. On balance I think it would be better to have either one or the other, that is, 18 for the legal and voting age or 21, but not both, because there is some pride in reaching manhood or womanhood and having a great measure of individual freedom. One of the great rights of freedom that we possess is that right to vote.
Then there is the question of the development of the human personality and the human body, the physical development and the physiological development. I suspect that 18 is too young an age to say that one has developed fully emotionally, mentally, physically or physiologically; perhaps 21 is too old, but I think 18 is too young.
If these thoughts still leave me in a quandary, Mr. Speaker, I would think that great care should be given to this measure. Whether we adopt it in principle or not, I still believe that the school of experience is an important one to evaluate and to take into account when we are considering the voting age of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this resolution I would like to say that the country I come from is vastly different from this country. Out there you can pass a farm and see a young man on a tractor. Quite often he is 15 or probably 16 years old; he might be 14. He can run a combine. He can do things that a young fellow 40 years ago, or even 30 years ago would never dream of doing.
When I was a youngster I lived in Arthur Meighen's constituency. I can remember going to political meetings throughout the country. I used to be cheer leader. They did not think we were smart enough in those days to have anything to do with politics, but we could line up at the front. They were all joint meetings in those days. Mr. Meighen was one of the most powerful speakers a man ever listened to and when it came time for him to speak we would sing: "What's the matter with father? He's

all right. I used to be a Liberal strong but now I see I'm in the wrong. What's the matter with Meighen? He's all right."
That was the extent of our political persuasions in those days and naturally we took a great interest in politics. But now we have the Indians voting and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) says that the young people should be able to vote. I come from the same kind of constituency that he does and I honestly believe that the young men and women should have the right to vote because a woman 18 years old is old enough to have a family and that is what counts. If the census had been made we could have learned a lot of things from it. I think that 18 is young but nevertheless I am in favour of the boy and girl of 18 having the right to vote. Perhaps we could reach a happy medium by setting the age at 19 or 19J.
Hon. members know what young people are like. Their ideas are vastly different from those of their elders and they are faster on the trigger. They want to get things done more quickly. About all I can say is that they should have the vote because the world is moving fast. Everything is on the go, on the jump. I hope the Conservatives will give the vote to the younger people because I am in favour of it and I am sure everybody else is.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to those who spoke either in favour or against extending voting rights to young people of 18. In my opinion, the right to vote is a sacred privilege that is used in this country after all due consideration by those who are periodically asked to elect new representatives every three, four or five years. Therefore, in the light of information they have obtained by listening to speakers at political rallies, after analysing the platforms of the parties, and often after discussing in private circles the platform of this or that party, they cast their votes according to the dictates of their conscience.
The mover of this bill showed a great interest in young people of 18 and asked us to grant them the right to vote.
I do not know whether a young person of 18 has enough maturity to use his vote in a way that is consistent with the general opinion. A party is often returned to power after a thorough analysis of the conduct of its leaders or because it has carried out its platform. The young people of today have to live in a modem era that, as was so rightly pointed out by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson), induces them to quicken the

pace of life. Therefore, I am wondering if we should not first of all give the young people in our high schools more schooling on the importance of the right to vote and its implications, particularly in view of the fact that a people always has the leaders it deserves. Before choosing those who will be responsible for running a country or a province, we must keep in mind that there are some responsibilities on the part of the voter, but think how much greater are the responsibilities of the politician who seeks a mandate from the people. In fact, during his term of office, he must quite often show endless devotion and courage. Well, today's youth do not show enough interest, unfortunately, in politics, because there may be a lack of information or education that prevents them from fully understanding the politician's role and duty.
Earlier, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) referred to the effects such a franchise could have on the civil code of the province of Quebec. Majority, which is reached at 21 years of age, gives to the individual, at that time only, the legal personality which entitles him to do something of legal value. Well, when the hon. member for Beauce referred to section 314 of the civil code of the province of Quebec, which deals with the enfranchisement of under-age people, I believe that he made his point too rapidly, because an enfrachised minor is still under the guardianship of his tutor. And enfranchisement by marriage does not involve the right of absolute majority in the province of Quebec. The right of majority, as recognized and enacted by the civil code of the province of Quebec, can only be obtained at the age of 21.
Why is it that our legislators considered that the right of majority can be obtained only at the age of 21? We may wonder whether experience has not justified such a policy on the part of our legislators who considered that before that age, normally, the individual has not reached full intellectual maturity.
