Mr. Chairman, before the debate on the resolution dealing with the construction of a railroad to Mattagami lake was adjourned, I had pointed out my previous mention of that district, when the estimates of the department of mines were discussed at the session of 1958.
If I may be allowed a brief digression,
I	emphasized, in my first speech the existence of the Mattagami lake district, stating that it would become as important as the Pine Point area in the Northwest Territories.
Later on, I met some people of my constituency who pointed out that I was wrong in saying that the district would become as important as the Pine Point one. According to them, I should have said that the new sector would be more important than Pine Point.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the resolution before us proves that they were right in being so optimistic, for its object is to authorize the building of the railroad thus giving a final character to the establishment of the district.
I might also stress the fact that on March
II	last, I called the attention of the minister of transport of the day to a statement which can be found on page 2063 of the French edition of Hansard for 1960.
I believe that this resolution, when it is enacted, will help remedy the present unemployment situation to a considerable degree because of the proposed railway construction work, and the fact that it will facilitate the setting up of numerous industries in that area.
Employment in Canada, Mr. Chairman, and more particularly in the northern district, is subject to seasonal ups and downs.
It is therefore normal that the number of unemployed should increase during the winter months.

Canadian National Railways
Consequently it would be essential to approve projects like this one which help open up new territories for our Canadian economy as well as prospects of a brighter future for Canada, especially for our young people.
The federal government, as everyone knows, enacted numerous pieces of legislation to curb unemployment and set the Canadian economy on the road to improvement. With the help of provincial and municipal authorities it will therefore be comparatively easy to create various temporary jobs, after those opened up by the winter works program. We expect business to pick up gradually. But this project will certainly contribute to increased employment. Because of its numerous possibilities, the proposal now before us will further help open up a good many territories, set up new industries and consequently increase employment.
In a general way, at various periods of our history, the mining industry has been subject to some fluctuations. It has had its good share of trouble. Yet, it has always managed to get out of trouble and take on new impetus. There are very extensive mineral deposits in the lake Mattagami area. As my colleague from the neighbouring riding pointed out in detail this afternoon, rather large deposits are to be found especially on the properties of the Mattagami Lake Mines, of the New Hoscoe Mines and the Orchan Mines. Up to now those three companies are the ones which have discovered the main deposits in the area.
Other companies too have made exploratory work and spent huge amounts of money for that purpose.
Other companies still might yet be successful, such as the Garon Lake Mines, east of Bell river.
All those companies, including the first three I mentioned and the Garon Lake Mines, have already found about one billion dollars worth of minerals in the area.
There are still other possibilities because many other mining companies have undertaken exploration work. I might even say that last fall a company made a new discovery some 30 miles west, according to the map I have here, southeast of lake Watson. This discovery which was mentioned during the debate this afternoon is likely to become rather important.
I think that the branch line that is being built right to the centre of this new mining district could be extended as far as Harri-canaw river, up to the Joutel township where this other discovery was made.
There are also other great possibilities of forest development in this vast area where large forests are still untouched.


There are also opportunities in the basin of the Allard river where new parishes may be established in a few years. In this territory, the land is highly suitable to agriculture and the climate is unusual, even a little better, I have been told, than in the southern part of Abitibi.
No doubt, because of the elevation in the neighbourhood of the Allard river in relation to sea level, the altitude is not as high as in the vicinity of La Sarre, Macamic, Amos or Senneterre.
Mention has been made also of the possibility of building a zinc refinery there, if possible, which would bring about an increase in population and the establishment of other secondary industries. Some neswpapers recently referred to the possible addition of a zinc refining unit at the Noranda mine, right in Noranda which is located in our area.
This would be better than nothing, of course, but the ideal solution for the future of the north and of this region especially would be the building of a local zinc refinery.
If a refinery were built, a city as large as Rouyn-Noranda could spring up in this vast territory of Abitibi.
There are still great possibilities to the north, as was pointed out this afternoon, and more especially along the Bell river and other rivers farther north, namely Bell river which becomes Nottaway river north of lake Mattagami, and also the East Main, Rupert and Broad Back rivers. In fact, they all have a vast potential for power production.
I am sure that this railway will be a first step toward the building of a line into James bay which should also be opened on the Quebec side. And that is the wish of the great majority, indeed of the entire population of northwestern Quebec.
I might also mention at this stage another kind of project which made headlines last year and this fall, and particularly since the opening of the new session, and I mean the Harricanaw waterway project. This project is still under study so to speak, but I think that before too long, it will command the special attention of the proper authorities, let alone the fact that it could easily be linked to the development of this vast territory, the success of which could be facilitated by the new railway, particularly if it were extended to James bay.
Before concluding my remarks, I would like to deal briefly with a particular point which was raised in the house a while ago. I raise this question because this afternoon, I listened to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who rather seemed to favour this project. This is a change in relation to what another member of his group,

the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) said in the house on May 23, 1958 as can be seen in Hansard for May 23, 1958.
The member for Timiskaming was then referring to the transfer of the Canadian National shops from Cochrane to Senneterre, due to the construction of the new branch line into Chibougamau. As a matter of fact, the new line to lake Mattagami would come under the new division in Senneterre. That is why I consider it advisable to mention the matter here, because there are in that text assertions which are altogether inaccurate and which must be corrected, in fairness, not only to the courageous population of Senneterre, but also to the entire population of Abitibi and to the proposed construction of the railway to Chibougamau.
Here is, in part, what he said on May 23, 1958, page 417 of Hansard:
For five years, the shop has serviced all the diesels and equipment operating in that division and the division in Quebec. It is now servicing 20 units a month and, with very little additional expenditure, those facilities could service 40 engines, more than are required in that area. To complete the modernization of the round-house would cost very little, but it is estimated it would cost about $1 million to build a new shop in Senneterre. This would represent $1 million more to be added to the loss which Canadian National is now incurring, in addition to these people being asked to move into a town which has no housing, nc suitable schools and no facilities in general for their reception. They are being asked to leave a place in which they have lived for many years, the reason given being that a new line has been built north into Chibougamau. I think anyone who has studied the financial papers during the last year will appreciate that if there is no change in the basic price for copper, that line will not be of much value to anybody. If copper prices fall much further, the tracks will be rusting before very long.
Mr. Chairman, I was anxious to challenge the unkind statement made about the town of Senneterre in my riding. Senneterre is directly connected to the new railway branch line toward lake Chibougamau and it will profit by it. This is a city which has prospered a great deal over the last years, and particularly since the war. A radar station was built there by the R.C.A.F. It is therefore untrue that the town lacks any of the required facilities, such as schools, streets, or sidewalks. Nothing is further from the truth, and I had to challenge such an incorrect statement.
I now wish to say a few words about another point, which in this case was raised this afternoon. I refer to the construction of a paper mill at Mattagami lake.

It has been stated in this house that the building of such a mill had been prevented by Mr. Duplessis. I have here the 1959 report of the committee on mines, forests and waters and I can show that such was not the case.
During a sitting of the committee, on May 19, 1959, while evidence was being given by Mr. M. I would say yes, in certain cases. I have in mind one in particular, in the province of Quebec. I cannot recall the name of the lake.
I thereupon suggested the name Mattagami and he said: Exactly, that is the area because the site proposed for the mill was too far away from transportation and no means of communication were then available. However, this problem will no longer exist after the construction of this branch line.

That was, in fact, Mr. Ambridge's statement before the committee.
Mr. Chairman, before I resume my seat, I want to pay tribute to the gigantic work performed by the pioneers in these vast territories. As a matter of fact, this area is more or less making its first appearance on the map and is just beginning to be spoken of. I think I am not exaggerating when I say that such a result is not the work of one man or of one government only. It is rather the work of a group of bold and clever men who settled in Abitibi, prospectors, engineers, mining promoters, professionals, forest workers, businessmen, farmers, and workers in all trades who made the development of our region possible.
It is to these pioneers that credit should be given for developing and expanding this

Canadian National Railways part of the Abitibi. Not only should they be congratulated for it, but tribute should be paid to them, because there is still so much land yet to be developed, from the inhabited portion of Abitibi up to the James bay area. The possibilities of the area are outstanding and we are just beginning to be aware of them.
Thanks to the new railway, the first step will have been taken and the development of these lands will be continued up to James bay. Our region will then experience a great revival that will profit not only the region itself but also the daring youth of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, it must be recognized that our young men and women have shown that they are capable of initiative.
I am just back from a visit to the mining cities of Chibougamau and Chapais in the northern part of my riding. Ten years ago these towns were non-existent. I am sure that following the construction of this branch line, numerous mining cities will be established, where our youth will turn to account their skills and contribute to the development not only of this region but of the province of Quebec and of the whole of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, it is unusual for a member from the Atlantic provinces to attempt to participate in such a debate. However, having a great interest in railway problems and particularly problems concerning the C.N.R., I feel it is proper for me to add a few words at this time.
In opening my remarks I wish to first of all congratulate the hon. member for Chapleau for his wonderful contribution to this debate. The hon. member in question is a resident of this area under discussion and has done much for the development of this part of the province of Quebec.
We have had many outstanding speeches on this resolution, particularly the speech of the hon. member for Roberval, which covered very well the background of the railway problem in this area.
Earlier today the hon. member for Laurier emphasized that the previous Liberal government authorized the C.N.R. to construct a total of 681 miles of railway lines during its term of office. The railway lines in question, together with their mileages, were itemized by the hon. member. I think it is appropriate for me at this time, as a member representing a railway riding, a riding dependent on the economy of the C.N.R., to state that in my opinion it is unfortunate that the list was so short not only in names but in miles. Mathematically it adds up to about 30 miles per year during their 22 years of office.
This short mileage is all that was constructed, notwithstanding the fact that the former government was in power during a period of war for five years, a period of depression of an equal length of time, and lastly during a period of prosperity unequalled in Canadian history, a period of boom when the government witnessed huge surpluses year after year.

The hon. member for Laurier emphasized that at times development in connection with railway construction in Quebec might not have kept pace with the development in the rest of Canada. He inferred that perhaps development in the area under discussion under the terms of this resolution was held back because of the wishes of the then premier of the province, the late Mr. Duples-sis. 1 do not know whether that is a fact or not, but as a former minister of the crown the hon. member for Laurier is perhaps more qualified than I am to make statements of that type. But I suggest that no government Liberal or Conservative should ever admit that a provincial premier since confederation, had enough influence on the federal government, because of fear or out of respect for a provincial premier, to fail to do anything which might have the adverse effect of holding up the development of any region of this country.
During a period of 22 years, as stated already today, the C.N.R. built a series of extensions or new mileage totalling 680 miles. A short line was built in New Brunswick known as the Bartibog extension. Whether that was a wise move economically remains to be seen, but that railway line was built under the regime of the former Liberal government at a time when we had a government in New Brunswick of a different political belief. It was fully supported by the federal government and the provincial government. Time will tell whether or not it was a good investment for the C.N.R.
I urge that the management of the C.N.R. should co-operate to the fullest extent with the provincial governments of this country and with the suggestions of business. I am confident that both provincial governments and business will now receive the kind of co-operation from the federal government to which they are entitled. The board of directors and the management of the railway should in connection with this particular project use their own forces where possible during construction. I realize that tenders must be called, but where possible C.N.R. employees should be employed. I also suggest that the management should instruct contractors to give priority to the employment of laid-off and former C.N.R. workers. I hope the Minister of Transport will be able to introduce this bill at the first opportunity and that it will receive a speedy passage through the committee stage.
In my opinion new railway lines must be developed in this country with speed. I suggest that a minimum of 100 miles a year would be a very conservative target for the C.N.R. and for the present government. This would make it possible to make up for the

Canadian National Railways lack of development which we have witnessed since the middle thirties. Apparently it was government policy when times were good, and during the war and post-war years, for the former government to do all it could by an unwritten policy to retard and hold up railway development in this country.
It appears from the debate that a smelter may be constructed somewhere in the St. Lawrence area. I believe that is the reason why the companies which have guaranteed a return to the railway have requested the extension of this line. This extension is justified. From what I understand, it is fully guaranteed from an economic point of view by the mining companies concerned. Perhaps the development of the Canadian north and the undeveloped areas of Canada will proceed with much more haste if it were possible for the government in its own right to cooperate with development companies by joining in the guaranteeing of returns when new lines are promoted. It is my belief that this country cannot again afford to be caught with poor planning such as we have witnessed during the past 20 years or so.
I suggest that the St. Lawrence seaway, a project which has done much for central Canada, is the reason for the resolution now before the committee. Possibly the subject under discussion could be compared to the problem of the development of the Chignecto canal in the maritime provinces. I believe it is related, because if the St. Lawrence seaway had any effect on the resolution it must be assumed that a canal in the Atlantic provinces would likewise justify more trade and promote prosperity, new smelters and perhaps secondary industry.
In conclusion I wish to congratulate the management of the C.N.R. on the foresight and co-operation it has shown. I also want to congratulate the company on its program in recent years for building the first hump yard in its system in the Atlantic provinces and for its new plans for the redevelopment of the Moncton area. I should also like to congratulate this government on its new policy of co-operation. Available transportation is the most elementary requirement for the economic development of any undeveloped region. It developed the east; it was a term of confederation, and this area of Canada affected by the resolution is now about to witness its goal-a horizon with an economic future.

subtopic: REPEAL OF TAX LAWS RESPECTING HALIFAX SIGNAL STATION
speechtext:
Yes, I have a short statement. This bill is for the purpose of removing from the statute books an act which has long outlived its usefulness. Its title is an act relating to the signal station at Halifax. It was enacted in 1859, under chapter 64 of the statutes of Nova Scotia, and assessed the sum of 5 shillings, and later $1 upon all steamers and other vessels which entered into the port of Halifax from ports outside of the province of Nova Scotia. Vessels owned in the province of Nova Scotia, except those registered and owned in the port of Halifax, were exempt from payment. In chapter 42 of the same statute of 1861 was an amendment exempting some of the vessels registered and owned in the port of Halifax. Chapter 66 of the statutes of Canada, 1908, was a further amendment exempting vessels under 115 net tons from the payment of signal dues.
The idea behind the bill, Mr. Speaker, is that at the time the statute was enacted a signal station was maintained on Citadel hill in Halifax where people kept watch over the sea by means of a telescope so as to be in a position to report as soon as a ship was in sight of the port of Halifax. Time was of the essence then because it was very important for the owners and operators of ships to learn as soon as possible when one of their ships was coming into port.
With the advent of radio this service was no longer required but the tax was still levied on all ships entering the port of Halifax. The tax amounted in total to $1,510 in the fiscal year 1959-60. It is felt that the collection of the tax is a nuisance and, in addition, the tax is not levied at any other port in Canada. At present the requirement to levy the tax is mandatory and the bill is required to eliminate it.
